reconcile.connective: Defenders read Horeb and Sinai as two names for one mountain — Horeb the broader desert range, Sinai the particular peak — so the two sets of texts describe a single place.

discrepancy.connective: For source critics following Julius Wellhausen the split is not stylistic but documentary: the mountain called Sinai in the J and P texts is consistently called Horeb in the E and D texts, marking out separate, independently composed sources rather than one unified account.

skeptic.name: Julius Wellhausen
skeptic.work: Prolegomena to the History of Israel
skeptic.attribution: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (Eng. trans. 1885)

excerpts.excerpt_text: these are names of one and the same mountain, at least of the parts of it; one part of it was called Horeb, from its being a dry desert and desolate place; and the other Sinai, from its bushes and brambles.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the contradiction: Gill explicitly equates Horeb with Sinai as two names for one mountain, the single strongest harmonization on the row.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Malachi 4:4
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, arguing Horeb and Sinai are two names for one and the same mountain (citing Jerome and Josephus to the same effect).
